title: The Custody Gap
body:
A Canadian pension fund holding a "Canadian-domiciled" Bitcoin ETF and a US allocator holding a spot Bitcoin ETF are not taking the same risk. One sits inside a single coherent custody regime. The other sits in a seam between two regulators, neither of which owns the whole picture.

OSFI's crypto-asset guideline sets capital rules — how much a bank or trust company holds against crypto exposure. It says almost nothing about how the coins are actually kept safe. That job falls to the CSA, whose custody expectations remain staff guidance, not binding rule.

Strip away the fund wrapper and look at where the bitcoin sits: Cidel Trust is the named Canadian custodian for major TSX-listed crypto ETFs, but it appoints sub-custodians — Gemini, Coinbase, and (as of July 2026) Anchorage Digital Bank. All three are US-chartered. None answers to OSFI or the CSA.

Compare that to the US: since September 2025, the SEC has anchored spot ETF custody inside a single, decades-old federal framework with one regulator holding clear enforcement authority.

For Canadian allocators evaluating crypto exposure, "Canadian-domiciled" is a wrapper-location claim, not a custody-quality claim. Ask fund managers for the full custody chain, not just the named custodian — and watch OSFI's guideline update landing this September.

The fund label says Canada. The custody chain says otherwise.

#Crypto #Bitcoin #OSFI #CanadianFinance #InstitutionalInvesting

title: The Stablecoin Detour
body:
Canada just passed its first stablecoin law. It won't actually govern anything until 2027.

Bill C-15's Stablecoin Act received Royal Assent in March 2026, giving the Bank of Canada supervisory authority over stablecoin issuers. But the detailed regulations are still being written — 12 to 18 months of rulemaking, expected in force in 2027.

In that gap, Canadian fintechs are settling real volume through US dollar stablecoins, because that's the infrastructure that already works at scale. Roughly 99.5% of the world's $308B stablecoin supply is USD-denominated. Regulated Canadian money service businesses like Paytrie already offer CAD-to-USDC conversion; Shakepay supports USDC directly.

Canada does have a homegrown answer: CADD, launched in May 2026 by Tetra Digital Group with National Bank, Shopify, Wealthsimple, and ATB Financial behind it — the first Canadian-dollar stablecoin from a regulated institution. It's a genuinely strong consortium. It's also months old, competing against a multi-year head start.

None of this requires a crisis to matter. It compounds quietly, transaction by transaction, in settlement flows already happening today.

Ottawa wrote the rulebook. The market didn't wait for it.

#Stablecoins #Fintech #BankOfCanada #DigitalPayments #CanadianFinance

title: The Open Banking Lag
body:
Canada is on track to become the last G7 country with a working consumer-driven banking system.

Bill C-15's Consumer-Driven Banking Act received Royal Assent in March 2026 — the first real legislation on this file since Finance Canada flagged it as a priority back in 2018. Detailed regulations followed in June, with a comment period that just closed. But the rollout is staged: Phase 1 (read-only access) is what's coming; Phase 2 (payment initiation, account switching) isn't expected until mid-2027, and depends on the Real-Time Rail, which is itself still not live.

Compare that to the UK: live since January 2018, now at 15+ million users and 2 billion+ API calls a month. Eight years of compounding adoption that Canadian fintechs simply haven't had access to, in their own market.

Fintechs Canada has been blunt about the cost: teams are still engineering around credential-sharing workarounds instead of building on standardized APIs, and every quarter of delay is a quarter of disadvantage against foreign competitors with a real head start.

Canada has finally written the law. It hasn't built the system — and Canadian fintechs, not just consumers, are the ones paying for the gap.

#OpenBanking #Fintech #CanadianBanking #BillC15 #Innovation

title: The Neobank Ceiling
body:
Neo Financial just raised $68.5M from more than 100 Canadian investors. Its valuation is still below where it was in 2022.

Koho, meanwhile, is spending its latest capital raise trying to become a federally regulated bank rather than stay a fintech. That's the clearest evidence Canada's neobanks have hit a structural ceiling — not a marketing problem, an architecture problem.

Two things cap the growth. First, CDIC deposit insurance: none of Canada's major neobanks are themselves CDIC members — they hold deposits in trust at partner banks, meaning the protection customers get is ultimately backstopped by a Big Six balance sheet, not the fintech's own. Second, revenue: Koho has said only ~1% of its revenue comes from net interest margin, versus ~50% for a traditional bank. Without a banking licence, a neobank can't lend against its own deposit base.

That's precisely why Koho is now in Phase 2 of an OSFI review pursuing what would be Canada's first new Schedule 1 bank licence in decades.

Wealthsimple, the sector's biggest success story, has $155.6B CAD in AUM and 3.6M users — and is majority-owned by Power Corporation, one of the institutions the neobank era was supposed to disrupt.

Canada's neobanks didn't fail to disrupt Big Six banking. They ran into the ceiling Big Six banking was built to have.

#Fintech #Neobanks #Wealthsimple #Koho #CanadianBanking

title: The Capex Multiplier
body:
Nvidia's stock price is not where the AI capex story shows up first in Canada. The transmission lines in Quebec and Alberta are.

Microsoft, Google, Amazon and Meta are on track for roughly $725B in 2026 capex, and a growing share is chasing cheap, reliable power, not just talent. Meta broke ground in July on its first Canadian data centre — a C$13B, 1-gigawatt facility north of Edmonton. Alberta's broader pipeline now totals 16+ gigawatts of requested capacity.

Quebec is running a more disciplined version of the same trade: Hydro-Québec is doubling its rate for large data centres specifically to capture the value of its renewable surplus, and CDPQ has already put $175M+ into a hydro-powered Quebec City campus.

Canadian pension funds aren't waiting for a thesis to form — CPP Investments committed $2.4B alongside EQT in July as part of a strategy targeting 10+ gigawatts of data-centre capacity globally.

Software carries the speculative multiple in this cycle because nobody knows which model wins. Power and transmission assets don't face that uncertainty — whoever wins still needs electrons delivered to a specific site.

The chips get the headlines. In Canada, the transmission lines are quietly getting the returns.

#AI #DataCenters #CanadianInfrastructure #Pensions #Investing

title: The Productivity Mirage
body:
Canadian firms tell pollsters AI is transforming how they work. Statistics Canada's productivity numbers tell a different story — two quarters running.

Business-sector labour productivity fell 0.5% in Q1 2026, the second straight quarterly decline, even as AI adoption among Canadian firms reportedly quadrupled from 3% to 12% since 2022. Hours worked actually rose 0.4% while output fell — the opposite of what widespread AI-driven efficiency would produce.

The Bank of Canada's own Business Outlook Survey shows firms citing AI integration as an investment priority, and a BoC staff paper found ~90% of AI adopters report no change to staffing — most are augmenting workflows, not automating them. Adoption is real. It just hasn't shown up in aggregate output yet.

The US comparison sharpens the puzzle: American nonfarm productivity rose 2.9% year over year in Q1 2026 and 2.2% in Q2, with the same technology and much of the same enthusiasm. The more defensible explanation isn't slower AI adoption in Canada — it's chronic underinvestment in capital per worker blunting the payoff even where the tools are in use.

The Bank of Canada's rate decision lands today. Weak realized productivity narrows how much room policymakers have to let demand run hot, AI optimism aside.

Enthusiasm shows up in surveys. Output shows up in GDP. Right now, only one of those is moving.

#AI #Productivity #BankOfCanada #CanadianEconomy #MonetaryPolicy

title: The Maple Mandate
body:
Canada's biggest pension fund now holds more in private equity and real assets than in public stocks. Most Canadians' RRSPs hold the exact opposite mix.

CPP Investments ended fiscal 2026 with $793.3B in net assets — 42% in private equity and real assets combined, versus 36% in public equities. PSP Investments' infrastructure book returned 17.8% for the year. Ontario Teachers' called out gold by name as a top return driver in both its H1 and full-year 2025 results, especially notable in a year when its private equity and real estate marks disappointed.

This isn't four funds hunkering down. It's where Canada's most sophisticated, longest-horizon capital has decided the next decade of returns will come from.

Retail Canadians are largely positioned the other way — still holding roughly half their equity portfolios in domestic stocks, in an index that's now 37% financials, an eight-year concentration high. Private infrastructure and gold, the two areas institutional allocators have been building out, are close to absent from the typical self-directed RRSP.

No retail investor needs to replicate a $793B asset mix. But when the entities with the deepest research budgets are deliberately reducing reliance on Canadian public equities, a portfolio still overweight the TSX isn't being prudent — it's just late.

#AssetManagement #CPPInvestments #Pensions #Gold #RRSP

title: The Home Bias Tax
body:
The TSX just posted a 31.5% total return in 2025. That's the worst possible moment to ask whether your home bias is paying off — because it's masking the real risk.

Canadian investors still hold roughly half their equity portfolios in domestic stocks, even though Canada is only 2.5-3% of global equity markets. That rally was powered almost entirely by two things: a bank-stock surge that pushed financials to 37% of the TSX, an eight-year high, and a gold price that roughly doubled in twelve months. Neither is a bet on Canadian earnings growth.

Add energy and materials, and well over half the index sits in three cyclical, commodity- and rate-sensitive sectors. An index that was supposed to give diversified Canadian exposure has quietly become a leveraged bet on bank earnings and gold prices.

The S&P 500's concentration runs through a different channel — the Magnificent Seven and roughly $700B+ in 2026 AI capex — which is a bet on earnings and productivity being reinvested into future output, not on interest rates staying favourable for lenders.

RRSP season is the one point in the calendar most Canadians actually look at their asset mix. This year, the question isn't "did I miss the TSX rally" — it's how much of that strength is genuine diversification versus a concentrated bet that happened to pay off.

Home bias isn't a mistake that shows up in a bad year. It shows up in a great one, disguised as vindication.

#Investing #TSX #PortfolioDiversification #RRSPSeason #CanadianInvestors

title: The Central Bank Floor
body:
Every G7 central bank treats gold as reserve insurance except one. Canada's holding: zero tonnes, for a decade running, while Poland, China and half the emerging world buy at the fastest pace on record.

The Bank of Canada finished selling its last gold in February 2016, closing out a five-decade wind-down that started in the 1970s. Every other G7 economy still holds meaningful bullion — the US near 8,130 tonnes, Germany/Italy/France a combined 8,200+, Japan around 840.

Meanwhile the World Gold Council's Q2 2026 data shows official-sector purchases of 288.9 tonnes, up 62% year over year and the strongest Q2 on record. 89% of surveyed reserve managers expect their institutions to add more gold over the next year. Poland alone added 82 tonnes as part of a stated plan to reach 700 — explicitly tied to security concerns on NATO's eastern flank.

The case for Canada's status quo isn't unreasonable — gold pays no yield, and no currency is realistically positioned to displace the US dollar as reserve currency anytime soon. But the driver of official-sector gold demand has shifted from an inflation hedge toward a sanctions and counterparty hedge, a risk category Canada's current reserve mix does nothing to address.

The floor under global gold demand isn't retail investors or ETF flows. It's central banks — and Canada is the one at the table with nothing on it.

#Gold #CentralBanks #BankOfCanada #ReserveAssets #Macro

title: The Miner's Discount
body:
Gold is up nearly 40% from a year ago. Barrick Mining's forward earnings multiple is still below the sector average, and the sector as a whole is trading at close to a 19% discount to net asset value. That gap is the trade.

Gold trades near $4,650/oz in late August 2026. Barrick and Agnico Eagle — the two TSX-listed miners large enough to move the index on their own — haven't repriced to match. Barrick's Q2 2026 earnings rose 74% year over year, cleared a major Newmont dispute, and the company is now spinning off its North American gold assets via a targeted NYSE IPO above $60B, explicitly to force the market to value a pure-play gold vehicle higher than a diversified miner.

Agnico Eagle posted record free cash flow of $1.34B in Q2 even as its stock sits ~40% below its March 2026 peak, largely on a temporary pit-wall issue at one deposit.

Three forces keep the discount alive: memory of the 2011-2013 cycle's capital destruction, jurisdiction risk on remaining African/South Asian exposure, and a gold rally that's flowed disproportionately through bullion vehicles rather than equities.

For a Canadian RRSP or TFSA already holding bullion exposure, adding miner exposure at an 11x forward multiple next to $4,650 gold is a bet the gap closes — not a bet on where gold goes next.

#Gold #Barrick #AgnicoEagle #MiningStocks #TSX
